summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would update Australia's migration laws to strengthen the use of biometrics for identity checks.
It would consolidate eight existing personal identifier collection powers into a single broad power to collect biometrics from non-citizens and citizens at the border.

The bill would also let officers collect personal identifiers from minors and incapable people without requiring consent or presence of a guardian, and would start within six months of royal assent if not proclaimed earlier.
changes: Consolidates and simplifies the legislative framework for collecting personal identifiers.
Expands collection powers to include minors and incapable persons without guardian consent.
Adds flexibility in how and where personal identifiers can be collected.
Removes unused and unnecessary provisions from the Migration Act.
summary.affected: Non-citizens and citizens at the border, and minors and incapable persons in immigration contexts.

speeches.speaker: Richard Marles
speeches.brief: The speaker announced Labor will not oppose the Migration Amendment (Strengthening Biometrics Integrity) Bill 2015 in the House but will reserve its position in the Senate pending the outcome of a Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee inquiry due on 5 June, citing concerns about privacy safeguards, particularly for minors and vulnerable people, and ambiguities around biometric data retention for Australian citizens.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Migration Amendment (Strengthening Biometrics Integrity) Bill 2015, arguing it streamlines biometric data collection to improve border security, counter terrorism and human trafficking, and cited over 9,000 fingerprint matches since the program began, as well as cases of Junaid Thorne and Khaled Sharrouf evading identification.

speeches.speaker: Luke Simpkins
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Migration Amendment (Strengthening Biometrics Integrity) Bill 2015, which expands biometric data collection and checks at borders to combat terrorism, identity fraud, and human trafficking, citing the case of Khaled Sharrouf using his brother's passport. The bill enables manual fingerprint checks using mobile devices and includes collection of biometrics from minors, which the speaker endorsed as necessary for national security.

speeches.speaker: Nickolas Varvaris
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Migration Amendment (Strengthening Biometrics Integrity) Bill 2015 is essential to consolidate and simplify biometric collection powers, including fingerprints, facial images and iris scans, to strengthen border security and counter terrorism. The bill streamlines seven existing powers into one broad discretionary power, allows collection from minors and incapable individuals without consent, and enables manual fingerprint checks at airports and seaports, citing the case of terrorist Khaled Sharrouf who used his brother's passport.

speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: The Migration Amendment (Strengthening Biometrics Integrity) Bill 2015 replaces seven existing biometric collection powers with a single broad discretionary power to strengthen border controls amid terrorism threats, with 33 million people expected to pass through Australia's eight international airports in 2015, rising to 50 million by 2020.
